claims.nodeLabel: Alien Reproduction Vehicle (ARV) / Flux Liner
claims.sourceText: William B. Scott, interview notes on 'Brad', https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript p 10, 1990-12-03
claims.text: THE WITNESS DISOWNS PART OF THE DRAWING. Shown McCandlish's sketches in December 1990, Sorensen says of the manned vehicle: 'this is probably the farthest from what I saw, and no, I didn't see anything with an intake up above the windows like this', and 'mark extrapolates a bit too much'. Of the saucer drawing he says the opposite: 'you've got a drawing, as accurate as I could get [the round, saucer-looking thing]. This dwg is so GD..accurate that I can't be much more specific than this.'

claims.nodeLabel: Alien Reproduction Vehicle (ARV) / Flux Liner
claims.sourceText: Scott interview notes transcript p 10, https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , 1990-12-03; Disclosure Project Briefing Document section 3.8.5, https://archive.org/stream/DisclosureProjectBriefingDocument/DisclosureProjectBriefingDocument_djvu.txt , 2000-12; arvp.co.uk FLUX 1988 page, https://www.arvp.co.uk/flux-01/ , read 2026-09-18
claims.text: THE SIZES HAVE DRIFTED, AND THE DRIFT RUNS ONE WAY, across three opened documents. The 1990 interview notes give 'The small one was like 20 ft, the next 60 ft. diameter and the next one,...maybe 120 ft. diam. Just a guess; don't hold me to that.' The April 2001 Briefing Document gives the smallest as 'about 24 feet in diameter at its widest part, right at the base', the next as '60 feet in diameter at the base', and 'the largest of these vehicles was about 120 to 130 feet in diameter'. The arvp.co.uk FLUX 1988 page, read 18 September 2026, gives 'one with a 130-foot diameter, another with a 60-foot diameter, and a smaller one measuring 24 feet in diameter', with no disclaimer. Each retelling is more precise than the last about a figure the witness explicitly refused to stand behind.

claims.nodeLabel: Alien Reproduction Vehicle (ARV) / Flux Liner
claims.sourceText: William B. Scott, interview notes on 'Brad', https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript p 10, 1990-12-03
claims.text: The 1990 primary document gives the three craft their nursery-rhyme names and the witness's own guessed sizes: 'This was a really interesting craft--there were three of them. When I walked into the room....well, I thought of something stupid--like a nursery rhyme: daddy bear, mommy bear, baby bear. Like they'd been put in a Xerox machine--the same proportions, just diff. sizes. The small one was like 20 ft, the next 60 ft. diameter and the next one,...maybe 120 ft. diam. Just a guess; don't hold me to that.'

claims.nodeLabel: Mark McCandlish
claims.sourceText: Scott interview notes, https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , 1990-12-11, read against the Disclosure Project Briefing Document section 3.8.5, https://archive.org/stream/DisclosureProjectBriefingDocument/DisclosureProjectBriefingDocument_djvu.txt , 2000-12 — DEMOTED from Tier 1 (node carries no primary-record URL); needs primary replacement
claims.text: The Frank Carlucci identification is his own labelled speculation, and the earliest opened document describes a different kind of man. His 2001 testimony gives the host as 'a tall, thin, white-haired man with glasses [and] an Italian-sounding last name', 'already a millionaire in his own right and was in civilian life again after having been either a Secretary of Defense or an Under-Secretary of Defense', followed by 'this fellow whom I speculate was probably Frank Carlucci.' William B. Scott's 1990 interview notes instead record Sorensen describing his host as a man who 'was in the Carter administration, and they wanted him on the Bush team', who 'is a very organized, straightforward, honest, etc. guy. In fact, he's a Democrat, which is not in keeping with the Bush admin. at all', and who 'Runs a business of injection molding and special materials...has about 6 businesses.' Frank Carlucci was the sitting Secretary of Defense on 12 November 1988, so neither 'in civilian life again' nor the injection-moulding businesses fits him on that date.

claims.nodeLabel: Norton AFB air show, 12 November 1988, and the alleged classified exhibit
claims.sourceText: William B. Scott, interview notes on 'Brad', https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript p 1, 1990-12-11
claims.text: The primary interview document places the account only 'in early Nov. 88': 'His account: Was invited to airshow at Norton AFB, Calif., in early Nov. 88; before B-2 rollout, and around pres. election time.' The exact date 12 November 1988 comes from McCandlish's 2001 testimony, not from the 1990 document.

claims.nodeLabel: Norton AFB air show, 12 November 1988, and the alleged classified exhibit
claims.sourceText: William B. Scott, interview notes on 'Brad', https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript pp 12 and 15, 1990-12-03
claims.text: On the claimed performance: 'the guy said that with this group of craft that, uh....they'd been everywhere in the universe, and there's no life', and 'Just take it for granted, we've already tested this thing. The speeds on this are seven to eight times the speed of light, and we've been everywhere--and there's nothing out there. We better take care of the earth.' The witness's own framing of the whole event: 'They were PR people--it was a sales thing!'

claims.nodeLabel: Norton AFB air show, 12 November 1988, and the alleged classified exhibit
claims.sourceText: William B. Scott, interview notes on 'Brad', https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript p 4, 1990-12-03
claims.text: The same document records the staging: 'They sort of staged it in several different rooms. Was one big hangar, but everything was parked so close that the wings would ...be above the others in the hangar', with 'metal rods as separators and hung black cloth on them', and 'It was like a showroom--just like a car showroom--good analogy!'

claims.nodeLabel: Norton AFB air show, 12 November 1988, and the alleged classified exhibit
claims.sourceText: William B. Scott, interview notes on 'Brad', https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript p 15, 1990-12-03
claims.text: The claimed provenance of the design, in the witness's own words on the same tape: 'They just said that they had come across some hardware ...tried to make contact with these....The [others] didn't want to make contact; they just wanted to deliver the news and leave, OK? But, back in 1947, we had just won the war, we felt pretty damned cavalier and we...attacked, basically, OK? Rather than fighting back, they just tried to destroy their stuff and get away; and they didn't get all of it destroyed.' He continues: 'Also said they couldn't really make those things that they found work. That they had to build their own...that this was built for our consumption, not theirs.' Asked 'so we just looked at theirs and built our own?' he answers 'uh-huh. Based on what was seen. So it was not like a great R&D breakthrough; it was just copying something they had seen, to the best of their abilities.'

claims.nodeLabel: Norton AFB air show, 12 November 1988, and the alleged classified exhibit
claims.sourceText: William B. Scott, interview notes on 'Brad', https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript p 2, 1990-12-03
claims.text: The 1990 document records the alleged exhibit's claimed purpose in the witness's own words: 'And that's what the whole [meeting] was for--appropriations of billions of dollars to develop new craft.' Asked whether he read it as a fundraising exercise: 'Yes; it was showing prototypes...or just vehicles of all different kinds that they wanted money for. So they were trying to impress us. Needless to say we were impressed!...[group had about 30 or so people who were invited].'

claims.nodeLabel: Norton AFB air show, 12 November 1988, and the alleged classified exhibit
claims.sourceText: William B. Scott, interview notes on 'Brad', https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript p 10, 1990-12-03
claims.text: The witness's own judgement of build quality, in the same passage that gives the sizes: 'They looked poorly built, compared to the other ones. They had been built by scientists who didn't know a hell of a lot about laying up composite materials or whatever' and 'the whole thing was just coated with thick, heavy lead paint. It was brushed on!'

claims.nodeLabel: Norton AFB air show, 12 November 1988, and the alleged classified exhibit
claims.sourceText: Disclosure Project Briefing Document, section 3.8.5, https://archive.org/stream/DisclosureProjectBriefingDocument/DisclosureProjectBriefingDocument_djvu.txt , 2000-12, read against Scott interview notes transcript p 2, https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , 1990-12-03
claims.text: McCandlish's 2001 testimony adds a claim the 1990 document does not contain: 'Brad said that in this exhibit at Norton Air Force Base, a three star general said that these vehicles were capable of doing light speed or better.' The 1990 document says the opposite about ranks present: 'I did NOT see any stars in there--like generals of any sort. If there had, I would have noticed that.'

claims.nodeLabel: Norton AFB air show, 12 November 1988, and the alleged classified exhibit
claims.sourceText: William B. Scott, interview notes on 'Brad', https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript p 5, 1990-12-03
claims.text: The 1990 document also carries a second, non-saucer exhibit in detail: an unmanned diamond or 'elongated football shape' craft, 'maybe 100-110 in length; maybe 60 ft. width', with 121 ports which the briefers said 'were 121 cylindrical nuclear weapons, and that they were similar in design to nuclear howitzer shells', of which 'they already had some flying units of this thing, and they showed some pictures of it.'

claims.nodeLabel: Norton Air Force Base, San Bernardino, California
claims.sourceText: William B. Scott, interview notes on 'Brad', https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript p 15, 1990-12-03

claims.sourceText: PDF metadata and URL path, https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , read 2026-09-18
claims.text: The scan's provenance before December 2024 is not established by anything in it. The PDF's own metadata gives /CreationDate 'D:20241017132510' and /Producer and /Creator both 'PDFium'; the file is 9,172,025 bytes over 31 pages with 31 embedded JPEG page images and zero embedded fonts, so it is a scan with no text layer; and it sits under /wp-content/uploads/2024/12/ on a site whose operator is not named. Who held the notes between 1990 and 2024, and how they reached that site, is not in the opened record.

edges.note: He is not a witness to the craft. He drew it from a friend's verbal description a week after the claimed event, and his 2001 testimony is where it acquires the names Alien Reproduction Vehicle and Flux Liner in print.
